findings.title: AES-CBC with a fixed all-zero IV, deliberately pinned across builds
findings.class: Generation of predictable IV with CBC mode
findings.evidence: crypto.dart:26 `static final enc.IV _iv = enc.IV.fromLength(16);` - a 16-byte zero-filled IV, static so it is the same value for every install, used for both seal (crypto.dart:30) and open (crypto.dart:35) in AESMode.cbc. The comment at crypto.dart:24-25 states the fixing is intentional.
findings.impact: CBC with a constant IV is deterministic: the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext. Composed with the constant key, the entire PIN space - 10^4 or 10^6 values - can be precomputed once and the sealed blob looked up, so recovery is instant rather than merely possible. Independently, identical sealed values across devices reveal that two drivers chose the same PIN. The ciphertext is also unauthenticated, so it is malleable.
findings.recommendation: Use AES-GCM with a fresh random nonce per operation, stored alongside the ciphertext - which also solves the upgrade concern in the comment, since the nonce travels with the value and never needs to be reproduced by a later build. If CBC must stay, generate a random IV per encryption, prepend it to the ciphertext, and add an encrypt-then-MAC layer.

triage.reason: There is no benign reading: IV.fromLength(16) allocates a zero-filled buffer, the field is static final, and the comment states the value is fixed on purpose. The stated reason (opening old values after an upgrade) is a real requirement solved correctly by storing the nonce with the ciphertext.
Nothing compensates: seal and open are the only crypto entry points in the component and both take the same constant _iv; no envelope format carries a per-value nonce.
The protected value is the driver's unlock PIN, which the file's own comment treats as a secret that must never leave the handset.

scope.established_by: Read every use of _iv; it is referenced by both crypto operations in the class and by nothing else in the component.
scope.narrowed_by: uploadFingerprint (crypto.dart:40-41) does not use this envelope, so it is out of this finding's scope.

searched.for: a per-operation IV, or an IV prepended to the ciphertext of seal
searched.found: both methods take the shared _iv constant; seal returns only .base64 of the ciphertext with no nonce attached

searched.for: an authentication tag, a version byte, or any envelope wrapping the sealed value before storage
searched.found: the base64 string is written and read verbatim, so the ciphertext is stored unauthenticated

findings.title: Full API response bodies are printed to the device log on every GET, in release builds too
findings.class: Sensitive information written to log file
findings.evidence: client.dart:66 `debugPrint('GET $path -> ${response.statusCode} ${response.body}');`, unconditional and outside any assert or kDebugMode guard. Flutter's debugPrint is a plain function that forwards to print, so it is not compiled out of a release build, and nothing in this component reassigns the debugPrint hook. post (client.dart:74-85) does not log, so this is one call site, not a policy.
findings.impact: Delivery manifests - recipient names, street addresses, delivery notes - land in logcat on the driver's handset. The realistic reader is someone with the unlocked device or an adb host, or a preinstalled/OEM process with READ_LOGS; ordinary apps cannot read another app's log since API 16, which is what keeps this low. No credential is exposed on this path because the token endpoint would use post, which does not log.
findings.recommendation: Remove the body from the log line, or gate the whole call on kDebugMode and log only method, path and status. If request logging is needed in production diagnostics, redact by field allowlist before printing.

triage.reason: debugPrint is not assert-stripped and the call has no kDebugMode guard; foundation is imported purely for this. The name suggests debug-only and the behaviour is not.
The logged bodies are the delivery records rendered at delivery_detail.dart:78-82 - recipient name and street address, personal data of third parties.

The second principal is anyone with local log access - an adb host the driver authorized, a privileged OEM log collector, or a device-support process. It is a narrow principal, reflected in the low severity, not an absent one.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every output call in the component; this is the only one.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the get path logs. post bodies (including anything sent to a token endpoint) are not printed, and ApiException.toString() deliberately omits the body.

searched.for: other logging sinks - print(, log(, debugPrint, a reassignment of the debugPrint hook, or a crash/analytics SDK receiving bodies
searched.found: one debugPrint call and nothing else; no analytics or crash-reporting dependency in pubspec.yaml

searched.for: whether the error path leaks the body a second way
searched.found: ApiException stores the body but its toString() prints only the status - that one is handled correctly, which makes line 66 an outlier

findings.title: followNext allowlists the host of a link-supplied URL but never its scheme
findings.evidence: deeplink.dart:33-36: `final target = Uri.tryParse(next); if (target == null || !_trustedHosts.contains(target.host)) return false; return launchUrl(target, mode: LaunchMode.externalApplication);` - target.scheme is never inspected. Verified against Dart's parser that non-http schemes carry an authority through this check: `intent://track.courier.example/#Intent;scheme=https;package=com.attacker;end` and a javascript:// form both yield host == 'track.courier.example'. Reachable from any unrecognised route: main.dart:72-73 `default: await DeepLink.followNext(link.params);`.
findings.impact: The app hands a link-supplied URI to an external handler with only its authority checked. The plausible abuse is an intent:-scheme URI whose authority satisfies the allowlist being resolved by a browser that supports intent URLs, i.e. intent redirection with a destination the app never intended.
findings.recommendation: Require target.scheme == 'https' alongside the host check, and reject URIs carrying userinfo or a non-default port. Prefer resolving the follow-on destination server-side from a delivery id rather than accepting a URL from the link.

triage.reason: The narrowing is real but partial: deeplink.dart:34 constrains the authority and nothing constrains the scheme. FP-11 would need the construct to apply to less than it appears; here one dimension is constrained and the other is wide open, verified by parsing two non-http URIs that pass the check.

What launchUrl(..., externalApplication) does with each scheme depends on the resolving app on the device, which a source review cannot settle. This is why the finding ships as probable and not confirmed.
next is a query parameter of an inbound VIEW intent, reachable through the unverified courier scheme filter.

scope.established_by: Read followNext line by line, found its only caller by reading the switch in _handleLink, and tested candidate URIs through Dart's own Uri parser to see which pass the check.
scope.narrowed_by: The host allowlist genuinely holds against the ordinary bypasses: https://track.courier.example@evil.example/ parses with host == 'evil.example' and is rejected. Only the default switch arm reaches this function.

searched.looked_in: courier_app/lib/util/deeplink.dart:29-37 (parsed candidate URIs through Dart's Uri)
searched.for: a userinfo or authority-confusion bypass of the host allowlist
searched.found: no bypass - the allowlist itself is implemented correctly; the gap is only the missing scheme constraint

searched.for: a route allowlist that would keep unknown routes away from followNext
searched.found: the opposite - default: sends every unrecognised route there

findings.title: The exported launcher activity declares no taskAffinity
findings.class: Improper restriction of rendered UI layers
findings.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:14-21 declares MainActivity with android:exported="true" and android:launchMode="singleTop" and no android:taskAffinity, so the affinity defaults to the package name. There is no android:excludeFromRecents and no HIDE_OVERLAY_WINDOWS usage anywhere in the manifest.
findings.impact: A malicious app that declares the same task affinity with allowTaskReparenting can place its own activity into this app's task, so the driver returns to the app and is shown the attacker's screen inside what reads as the courier app - the delivery vehicle for a credential or PIN phishing prompt. Recent Android versions mitigate the classic variants, which is why this is low.
findings.recommendation: Set android:taskAffinity="" on MainActivity so it is never a reparenting target, and confirm minSdk/targetSdk in the Gradle configuration that is not part of this component.

triage.reason: Whether the shipped build's minSdk leaves a materially exposed install base cannot be established: the component contains no build.gradle, and the source cannot tell what the merged manifest declares. This caps the finding at probable.

exported="true" is intended and bounded - the activity is the launcher and carries MAIN/LAUNCHER - but per FP-05 the finding moves rather than disappears: what sits behind the intended exposure is the missing affinity hardening on that same activity.

The platform mitigations on Android 11+ are a compensating layer in another domain, but no artifact establishes which platform versions this build supports, and 'the platform takes care of it' without evidence is not a HOLDS.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every attribute of the single <activity> element and listed which platform-hardening attributes are absent.
scope.narrowed_by: RouteTrackingService is exported="false" and is not affected; there is only one activity in the manifest.

searched.for: taskAffinity, excludeFromRecents, allowTaskReparenting or a singleInstance/singleTask mode that would change the exposure
searched.found: none of them; launchMode is singleTop and affinity is left at the package default

searched.for: a Gradle file or a <uses-sdk> element establishing minSdk/targetSdk
searched.found: neither exists - the manifest declares no <uses-sdk> and there is no build script, which is why this stays probable

findings.title: Dependencies are declared as floating caret ranges with no lockfile present in the component
findings.class: Inclusion of functionality from an untrusted control sphere
findings.evidence: pubspec.yaml:12-21 declares nine direct dependencies, every one a caret range: http ^1.2.1, flutter_secure_storage ^9.2.2, webview_flutter ^4.8.0, encrypt ^5.0.3, crypto ^3.0.3, app_links ^6.1.1 and three more. No pubspec.lock is present in the component as delivered.
findings.impact: Without a committed lockfile, flutter pub get resolves to whatever newest matching version exists at build time, so the security-relevant code that ships - the WebView host, the secure-storage implementation, the cipher - is not determined by the repository, and a compromised or regressed upstream release enters the build silently.
findings.recommendation: Commit pubspec.lock (it is expected for an application, and publish_to: none at pubspec.yaml:3 confirms this is an application), and verify it in CI with flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile so a build cannot silently resolve differently.

triage.reason: It cannot be established that no pubspec.lock exists in the real repository - a nine-file component was given and the file is absent from it, which is weaker evidence than a listing of the repository. UNKNOWN caps this at probable, and the artifact that would settle it is named.
Caret ranges in pubspec.yaml are normal and intended practice; the exposure they create is bounded only by a lockfile, so the finding moves to that lockfile rather than disappearing.

scope.established_by: Enumerated pubspec.yaml key by key and listed every dependency constraint individually.
scope.narrowed_by: The two sdk: flutter dependencies are pinned by the SDK and are not affected. environment.sdk is a bounded range and is fine.

searched.for: pubspec.lock, or a CI step enforcing it
searched.found: neither is present in the component - which holds this at probable rather than confirmed

searched.for: bundled assets that could ship a credential or config file
searched.found: only assets/icons/ - no .env, no config JSON, no key material declared as an asset
